Fig. 3.  The obstruction pairwise reasoning cannot see. Every pair of worlds admits a safe coordinate; no coordinate works for all three.

A class contains a safe tips and b unsafe tips in a finite set T. A world is the unsafe set W ⊆ T with |W| = b. Observations reveal only unsafe tips, so a transcript is a revealed subset R ⊆ W. The task is to name a safe tip, not to identify W. That distinction is the point.
The question is how much cheaper deciding is than recovering, and whether the natural decoder — name a tip drawn uniformly from the unexplored set — is actually optimal or merely convenient.
What the literature leaves open

The literature therefore leaves a specific opening. Decision-region determination designs policies and gives approximation ratios but not an exact optimality statement for a terminal decoder; minimax decision theory supplies the chain but was not run to completion for this problem; coupon collection supplies the recovery cost but not an exact comparison.

No existing treatment simultaneously: (i) proves the decoder's risk depends on the transcript alone; (ii) establishes optimality over all decision rules with the infimum attained; (iii) derives the constant-risk property from symmetry rather than assuming it; and (iv) exhibits a decide–recover separation in which the decide side is an identity independent of the number of classes.
II.  Methodology
Every statement displayed below is machine-checked, with no unproved step anywhere in the chain. STEP 1 — THE SAMPLING LAW  (C5). HOW IT IS CLOSED.

Step 1 gives what a transcript reveals; Step 2 asks what a decoder can do with it. The key counting fact is that every world compatible with a transcript has exactly b unsafe tips and contains all revealed ones, so the number still hidden is the same in all of them:
HOW IT IS CLOSED.  A cardinality computation on the compatible worlds, then division by the size of the unexplored set.
HOW IT IS CLOSED.  Exchanging the sum over worlds with the sum over observations, then collecting the rule's action at each observation.
HOW IT IS CLOSED.  Each summand is at least the pointwise minimum over actions, and the bound is ATTAINED by choosing an argmin at every observation — a rule that.
HOW IT IS CLOSED.  Two inequalities composed.
HOW IT IS CLOSED.  In the symmetric model the decide risk collapses to an exact closed form that does not mention K at all, while the recovery count is bounded below by.
Fig. 4.  What one revealed tip is worth. Each revelation removes a term from numerator and denominator at once, so the curve is convex: the last few revelations carry most of the risk reduction.
III.  Results

DECIDING IS FLAT IN K; RECOVERING IS NOT. Across the parameter grid the exact decide count is independent of the number of classes while the exact recovery count grows, and the ratio between them grows without bound as K increases. Both counts are exact integers computed from the closed forms, not simulated. THE DECODER IS OPTIMAL, NOT MERELY FLAT.

With Step 5 the equivariant decoder is a least element of the achievable worst-case risks, so no decision rule whatsoever — randomised or not, adaptive or not — achieves a smaller worst case on this problem.
Fig. 1.  Samples to reach tolerance 1/100 for deciding (dotted) and recovering (solid). The decide lines are horizontal because K does not enter the formula.

Reporting Protocol All twelve cells are reported with no exclusions. Deciding Is Flat in K; Recovering Is Not At P=12 and ε=1/100, deciding takes 6 samples whether there is one class or thirty-two. Both columns are exact integers obtained by inverting closed forms.
IV.  Discussion

THE SEPARATION OVER THE WHOLE GRID, NOT TWELVE CELLS. 1080 cells reaching 1024 classes. At P = 1/2 and ε = 1/100, recovery costs the same 6 samples as deciding at one class, 17 at two, and 22,192 at 1024 — a factor of 3699. The separation is not an overhead a larger budget absorbs; it widens without bound. THE GROWTH HAS A SHAPE.

Fitting N_rec ≈ c·(K/P)(ln K + ln 1/ε) over each of 54 (P, ε) slices gives c between 0.916 and 0.966 with R² at least 0.99996 — the coupon-collector scale quoted for orientation is the right one, with a constant just under one. THE IDENTITY AGAINST THE PROCESS IT DESCRIBES.

Simulating the process and comparing: over 200 cells the measured value differs from the identity by at most 0.0043 and 2.98 standard errors, which over that many cells is what the null predicts. ONE THING NOT TO MISREAD. The flatness of the decide cost in K is STRUCTURAL: K does not appear in the formula.
Limitations — what is not established

One prior, not a minimax theorem. The prior is arbitrary but fixed: this is minimaxity through one Bayes prior, and no saddle point is claimed. What is obtained is a value lower-bounding the worst-case risk of every rule and achieved by one, which is the definition of a minimax-optimal rule; what is not obtained is a least-favourable prior. Everything is finite.

Attainment of the pointwise minimum is immediate in a finite action set; with an infinite one the conclusion weakens to an infimum that may not be achieved. The ease is in the proof rather than the statement — the earlier treatment had the same finite setting and not the result — but the limitation is real for any extension. The decoder is not uniquely optimal.

With an asymmetric prior the identification of the argmin with the uniform decoder fails, so Theorem's conclusion about that decoder no longer follows. The separation is model-specific. Theorem holds on a_i=b_i=1 with total unsafe mass fixed.
Nothing here designs the sampling, which is exactly what the decision-region literature does; the two are complementary rather than competing.
V.  Conclusions

Deciding and identifying are different problems, and the gap between them is not an overhead a larger budget absorbs. The decoder is minimax over ALL decision rules, not merely flat; the decide cost is exactly ½(1−P)^N and contains no K; and recovery grows on a coupon-collector scale with a constant just under one, reaching 3699 times the decide cost at 1024 classes.
How the numbers were produced

PRECISION IS SET FROM THE PROBLEM, NOT PICKED. The recovery sum alternates with binomial weights and loses about K bits to cancellation — at K = 128 the largest term already exceeds the answer by eighteen orders of magnitude. Working precision is therefore 120 + ⌈K·log₁₀ 2⌉ + 40 digits, 469 at K = 1024. A fixed precision would return noise at the top of the grid.

The recovery risk at K = 1 must equal the decide risk exactly in rational arithmetic — the one point where the two sides must agree. The high-precision and exact-rational evaluations must agree. And the sandwich ½·Pr(U>0) ≤ R_rec ≤ Pr(U>0) must hold. All three do.
